title: We Are the 'Custodians of Their Destinies'
author: Amy Coombe
summary: Amy Coombe, continuing a series on the attributes required to successfully lead a school reading programme, argues that determination is the quality most needed to sustain reading intervention against the specific obstacles that erode it over time. Opening from Dianne McGuinness's line that 'the teacher of the young reader is the custodian of their destiny' and the core principle that 'no one fails,' she catalogs five recurring obstacles: building genuine shared belief in reading's importance across a staff, resolving the tension between curriculum breadth and foundational catch-up (especially the pressure to abandon reading intervention for older students facing GCSEs), creating protected leadership capacity, ensuring only excellent, committed teachers deliver the programme regardless of subject specialism, and removing the attendance barriers that specifically affect the students reading intervention is meant to serve. For each obstacle she offers concrete, field-tested preemptions, from recording students reading aloud to build staff urgency, to releasing students from behavioral inclusion early so they don't miss reading lessons. Her sharpest and most counterintuitive claim is that Year 10 and 11 students, often abandoned by reading intervention in favor of exam preparation, are in fact the most vulnerable to illiteracy's effects given that the average GCSE paper has a reading age of nearly 16.
points: Coombe's sharpest counterintuitive claim: Year 10 and 11 students are the most vulnerable to reading gaps, not the least, because the average GCSE paper's reading age (15 years 9 months) makes exam access itself dependent on reading ability schools have often stopped supporting by that point.

She reframes reading versus curriculum breadth as a false tension: 'Reading is not an alternative to the curriculum; it is the means through which students access the curriculum,' repositioning reading intervention as infrastructure rather than a competing priority.

Her staffing recommendation deliberately breaks the assumption that reading intervention belongs to English specialists, arguing belief, commitment, and openness matter more than subject expertise for reading teachers.

The attendance preemption, releasing students from internal inclusion early enough to attend their reading lesson rather than missing it as a side effect of behavior sanctions, targets a specific, concrete failure point most reading strategies overlook.

The five-obstacle structure functions as a practical audit tool: a school leader can use it to diagnose exactly where a reading strategy is likely to stall, rather than treating implementation failure as a single undifferentiated problem.
quotes: The teacher of the young reader is the custodian of their destiny. Dianne McGuinness. We must internalise this truth. The quality of our reading teaching will determine whether doors open or remain closed.

McGuinness rightly argues that a core principle of an effective remedial programme is that it works for everyone at all ages. No one fails. This is such a crucial insight that I feel the need to repeat it: No one fails.
Reading is not an alternative to the curriculum; it is the means through which students access the curriculum.
The average reading age of a GCSE paper is 15 years and 9 months, so our students in Y10 and Y11 are actually the most vulnerable to the impacts of being unable to read.

Reading teaching is often considered the preserve of the English department, but the most important prerequisites for successful reading teaching don't involve English subject expertise; belief, commitment and openness are much higher priorities.
Getting a reading intervention working well is no mean feat! It takes fierce determination. But if we don't act with urgency, we risk condemning our students to a lifetime of missed opportunities.
